segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did. Sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because the mindset of the flesh is hostility toward God; for it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, the one who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, brothers and sisters, we are debtors—but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I consider that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation in eager expectation awaits the revealing of the sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly but because of the one who subjected it, in hope

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that the creation itself will also be set free from slavery to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering the pains of childbirth together until now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit—we too groan within ourselves as we await adoption, the redemption of our bodies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in this hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what they see?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with wordless groans,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the one who searches hearts knows what the mindset of the Spirit is, because he intercedes for the holy ones as God wills.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all—how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? God is the one who justifies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is the one who will condemn? Christ is the one who died—or rather, who was raised—who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we have been considered sheep for slaughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But in all these things we are more than conquerors through the one who loved us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.note: The Greek text followed here reads a singular “you,” found in several of the earliest manuscripts. Many other manuscripts read “me,” continuing the first-person voice of chapter 7, and a few read “us.” Editors are divided, and the sense of the passage is little affected.

Paul uses “flesh” in this chapter not for the physical body as such but for human nature in its weakness and under the dominion of sin, set against life directed by God’s Spirit. Some modern versions paraphrase it as “sinful nature” or “human nature.” The traditional word is kept because Paul’s contrast of flesh and Spirit depends on it.

The Greek is literally “and concerning sin.” In the Greek Old Testament this exact phrase is the regular term for the sin offering, and many scholars think Paul’s readers would have heard it that way. Others take it more generally as “to deal with sin,” and many English versions have simply “for sin.”

The Greek word can mean God’s Spirit or the human spirit, and Greek manuscripts do not distinguish them by capital letters. Many translations take it as the human spirit, “your spirit is alive.” The Greek says “life,” not “alive,” and the next verse speaks of God’s Spirit giving life, which is why the Spirit is preferred here; the question is disputed.

notes.phrase: because of his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.traditional: through his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between two grammatical forms that differ by a few letters. The Greek text followed here means “because of his Spirit”; the other reading, adopted by most English versions, means “through his Spirit.” The first makes the indwelling Spirit the reason for the future giving of life, the second the means; the evidence is closely balanced.

The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as members of one family. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations render it “brothers and sisters,” while others keep “brothers.” The same rendering is used in verse 29.

Paul uses “sons” here and in verse 19 but “children” in verses 16, 17 and 21, and the translation keeps the two words distinct. “Sons” ties in with the legal language of adoption and inheritance in verses 15 to 17, since in the ancient world an adopted son became an heir. Paul plainly includes women as well as men, and several modern versions translate “children” throughout.

The same Greek word stands behind “a spirit of slavery” and “the Spirit of adoption.” The second is taken here as God’s Spirit, who brings about adoption, in line with verses 14 and 16; some translations use lowercase “spirit” for both, meaning a disposition. The word for adoption is a legal term for the formal placing of someone as a son and heir.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the language of the Greek Old Testament for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

notes.phrase: all things work together for good
notes.traditional: all things work together for good
notes.note: The Greek can be read with “all things” as the subject, as here, or with God as an unexpressed subject: “he works all things together for good.” Some early manuscripts add the word “God” to make the second reading explicit; the Greek text followed here does not. Either way Paul’s point is that God’s purpose stands behind the outcome. The word “his” before “purpose” is supplied for English.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for hardship or oppression pressing on a person. “Tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. English versions vary widely here, using “trouble,” “hardship,” “affliction” and “tribulation.”

The word is the ordinary Greek term for a ruler or a ruling office. Standing between “angels” and “powers,” it most likely refers here to spiritual powers thought to hold sway over the world, not to human governments, though Paul does not spell this out. “Principalities” is the older English rendering; several modern versions have “rulers,” and some paraphrase as “demons.”

candidates.reason: Paul’s ethical sense recurs across the letters and versions split between “flesh,” “sinful nature” and “human nature,” so readers need one consistent rendering.
The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout Acts and the letters, and “brothers” versus “brothers and sisters” must be settled once.
The plural used of believers (“sons of God”) is rendered “sons” by some versions and “children” by others, and it needs to stay distinct from τέκνον consistently.
It recurs widely and is variously rendered “patience,” “endurance,” “perseverance” and “steadfastness.”
“Elect” versus “chosen” varies between versions and carries theological weight across the Gospels, Paul, 1 Peter and Revelation.

warnings: Verse 32: παραδίδωμι is not rendered with a register form (hand over; hand on; hand down; give up; give over; entrust; risk; be ripe) and has no register-exception note.
